# Dead Letters

The Dead Letter Office occupied the basement of the central post office, which everyone agreed was fitting, since its business was with things that had sunk.

Edith had worked there for nineteen years. Her job was to open mail that could not be delivered — no address, illegible address, addressee deceased, addressee never existed — and attempt, through the contents alone, to find it a home. There were rules. She wore gloves. She logged everything. She was not permitted to answer the letters, though no rule said she couldn't read them twice.

Most of what came down the chute was banal: birthday cards that missed their window, utility bills chasing people who had moved on, coupons expiring quietly in the dark. But every week brought something else.

A man wrote monthly to his wife at an address that had been demolished in 1987. The letters were cheerful, mostly — the garden, the neighbor's dog, his hip, which was better than the doctors predicted. Early on, Edith had looked up the demolition records and found the wife's name in an obituary dated three years prior. He knew. She was almost certain he knew. The letters weren't confusion; they were correspondence with a place.

A child mailed a tooth to the Tooth Fairy, care of "the Moon, probably." No return address. A woman sent back an engagement ring with eleven pages explaining exactly why, each page numbered, as though she feared the argument would arrive out of order. Someone mailed a recipe card — just the card, no note — for a soup that took two days to make, addressed to "My Son, wherever he's eating badly these days."

Edith kept a box, against regulations, of things like these: drawings addressed to God, apologies addressed to retired teachers, a marriage proposal addressed simply to "the woman on the 6:40 train who laughed at my newspaper." She couldn't deliver any of them. She couldn't throw them away either. There ought to be a word, she thought, for mail that arrives nowhere — not lost, exactly. Delivered to the basement of the world.

Then one Tuesday in November, an envelope came down the chute addressed to:

EDITH MARSH
THE PERSON WHO READS THE LETTERS THAT CANNOT BE DELIVERED
BELOW THE POST OFFICE

Her hands did something complicated — went cold, then hot. She checked the log. It had arrived through the regular stream, postmarked from a town four hours north, the stamp affixed slightly crooked, the way stamps go when someone is hurrying or crying.

She sat with it for most of her shift. Rules existed for this, presumably, though nineteen years had not prepared her for the category. Finally she opened it, because opening was her job, and because not opening it would have been unbearable.

*Dear whoever you are,* it began. *I don't know your name. My mother worked in a dead letter office when I was young — maybe yours, maybe another city's; she never said which. She died in March. Going through her things, I found forty-one letters, all opened, all undeliverable, all from my father, who left when I was six and whom I have spent thirty years believing never thought of me again. He wrote every month until he didn't. She read them all. She kept them all. She never gave me a single one.*

*I am not writing to ask why. I think I understand why, or I will someday. I'm writing because those letters were technically dead — undeliverable, unclaimed — and yet they were the most alive things in her apartment. And I thought: somebody opened those first. Somebody read them before she did, judged them worth saving, sent them on to her. Somebody was the first witness. I have been trying to picture that person for weeks. I hope it was you. I hope your work feels small some days, because mine does, and I want to believe that small work can hold a whole life inside it without knowing.*

*That's all. You needn't write back. I didn't leave an address, so you couldn't if you wanted to, and I know that's unfair, and I'm doing it anyway, because this isn't really a letter. It's a thank-you note with nowhere to go, and now it's yours.*

She read it four times. Then she did something she had never done in nineteen years: she took off her gloves.

Not dramatically. Just — the paper was warmer than she'd expected. That was all. Paper holds heat longer than you'd think, especially paper carried in a pocket to the mailbox, held awhile at the curb by someone deciding.

She logged it, per procedure. In the disposition column she wrote: *Delivered.*

Afterward, the work continued as it always did. Missives to saints, invoices to ghosts, love with insufficient postage. But Edith noticed she handled each envelope differently now — slower, the way you handle something already broken, or something not broken yet. Every letter, she understood, was written by someone standing at a curb somewhere, deciding. Her basement was only the deciding's last stop. Upstream, every message began as a living thing, warm from a pocket, and hers was merely the place where warmth went to wait.

So she waited with it. That seemed like the job, really, beneath the job.

On Fridays she still added to the box she wasn't supposed to keep: the tooth, the drawing of God as a lighthouse, the proposal for the woman on the 6:40 train. Sometimes she imagined a future clerk finding the box decades on, lifting each item with careful gloved hands, puzzling over where such things could possibly belong. She hoped they would reach the only conclusion available.

*Delivered,* she hoped they'd write. *Delivered, delivered, delivered.*
